

**Capstone Portfolio**  
Interactive Web Game For Elementary School  
ESOF 423 \- Fall 2026

Ridley Christoferson, Rebecca Edwards, David Knauert

**Section 1: Program**

At the beginning of this semester, our group had the idea to create an interactive coding web app for elementary aged students to get interested in coding. We had noticed through our experience that a lot of the coding done in early elementary was too convoluted and typing-oriented for the students to truly grasp what coding was, and staying interested beside the confusion was almost impossible. To bridge this gap between interest and confusion we decided to create a game that would keep them wanting to learn.   
	Our client is Mrs. Amy Defrance, a 5th grade teacher at Hyalite Elementary. She took interest in our project because she needed something to give her students who were excelling in speaking and reading skills while she worked with the students who need a little bit of extra help. 

**Section 2: Teamwork**

Team Member One:  
Team member one has mainly focused on level integration. They were in charge of implementing the logic for five of the game’s levels. Team member one has also helped with brainstorming ideas for the project. They helped figure out game features and how to implement some of the features.  
Team member one worked on finding a way to get the reward button to display when a level is completed. They are also working on figuring out how to get the avatars to display on the home screen once a level is  completed and a new character is unlocked.

Team Member Two:  
Team member two focused mainly on the server hosting and backend side of the web application using firebase. They got the group set up with firebase and implemented it into our web application so that it could run and be accessed by anyone with an internet connection on a url, as opposed to having to host the files locally from one’s computer. They also focused on getting users the ability to log in with their own personal email and save progress so that the application could be exited, logged back into, and played at the users own personal pace.  
At the beginning, team member two also helped design the concept of the game, pitching ideas for sprite customization and the homescreen ‘Zoo’ vibe. They helped with other team members to map out a plan for the outline of our game at the beginning of the semester, and continued to work towards a finished product throughout the course of the semester.

Team Member Three:   
	Team Member Three had a very organizational job in this project. From coordinating meeting times and explaining our project to our client to setting up the tasks to complete during the sprint based on user feedback, Team Member Three made sure the project was always progressing in a way that was valuable to our client and that our users feedback was constantly being implemented because, at the end of the day, our goal for this project is to help students learn.   
	As a secondary education major, this team member also contributed to the overall goals and outline of the project. They answer questions like, “How should levels progress?” “What is the outline of our levels” and “How do we actually teach these students the topics we’re trying to teach?” They came up with the 14 level progression, and the idea to create informational cards in the lessons before introducing the challenges to students.

**Section 6: Design Trade-Offs**

One significant design tradeoff we faced was the setup of our levels when it comes to coding within our web application. Considering we are working on a coding education game, we had to decide how our clients (students) would be coding within the browser on our website (since it is not an IDE).

The choice lies in how much freedom you give the students with how much they can customize and expand their coding. We decided that having a full level interpreter that can translate their pseudo-code into a real coding language (and then be able to run that real code and have the students see their results) was too big a task for the scope of this project.

However, we also did not want the students to only be reading about programming concepts and not get any hands-on practice with writing code and executing it, as we believe this is one of the most fun and educationally rich aspects of learning about programming. We wanted students to be able to do both, that is: read about programming concepts as well as practice writing code, even if the latter is at a lower level than what would be possible in a full scale IDE.

We executed this by having educational ‘cards’ that students flip through at the beginning of each level in order to get some crucial background on that level's content. Then, we provide some opportunity for the students to do some basic coding (like writing loops, functions, and conditional statements). The tradeoff is that we check and ‘run’ student input strictly by comparing their code (as a string) to what we have as the correct answer. There is some flexibility, as we can have them input different numbers into a loop and have a different output in the movement of their sprite as a result. However, we cannot have students write separate, personalized, or complicated blocks of code in a sandbox sort of fashion.

This was something limited by the time constraints of the project as well as our knowledge as undergrads when it comes to creating an entire interpreter by ourselves. We supplemented this drawback by providing students with a fun and unique foundation for programming education and then referring them to more resources where they can use their skills to create large, individual projects (like w3schools or code.org).

**Section 7: Software Development Life-Cycle Model**

The software development model we used for this project was the agile model with the scrum  
Methodology. At the beginning of each sprint, one group member was assigned as the ‘scrum master’ who is tasked with facilitating meetings and making sure the group gets their sprint goal done by the end of the two weeks.

This worked pretty effectively for us, as the sprints served as effective milestone markers throughout the course of the semester to ensure that we had something to show our professor, classmates, client, and ourselves, even if it felt unfinished at some points. It was a way to make sure we had something rather than nothing, which is always the better option.

One struggle of integrating the Agile development model into our situation was the amount of in person time we had together compared to people working at an actual software company. In our case, we had two hour long blocks during class to meet and discuss, and the rest was left to be done outside of class time. This was challenging because we are all busy college students with other classes, jobs, and time commitments, and couldn’t find much time to work together outside of class besides texting updates of our progress. This leads to work feeling much more individual and less focused than it would in a real software development job. 

Nonetheless, it served as good practice for using the Agile methods and seeing a glimpse into the workflow we would face in a real software development environment.
